title: ‘Now is not a good time’. So when, then?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino starts from a children's book and her son's remark about her own habit of saying not now, then asks whether schools say the same about professional development during the pandemic. Staff are stretched, yet she argues that some CPD focused on improving teaching, such as quality questioning or regular homework, should continue. Her reasons are that there is never a perfect time, that improving practice benefits learning, and that stressed teachers revert to automatic and often poor habits, citing research on habit formation. As a non-leader with school-wide responsibilities, she offers four conditions for leaders: evidence-informed focus, weighing impact against workload, listening to staff, and committing to review and refine. Her conclusion is that improving practice matters more, not less, in hard times.
points: Waiting for a calm moment to do CPD means it never happens, because there are always other deadlines.
Stress pushes teachers back toward automatic habits, so continued professional development guards against bad habits hardening.
CPD should be evidence-informed and should not be extensive marking or mandated slide formats.
Leaders should weigh impact against workload, listen to those implementing the change, and review and refine the focus as barriers emerge.
quotes: There will always be deadlines and jobs that need to be completed. Even before the pandemic, focusing on improving the quality of our questions or making homework a part of our teaching routine would have taken up thinking and planning time. If it is an important enough focus, then it is worth investing time in it.
When we are stressed, we tend to respond to events automatically, without as much careful thought as when we are not stressed (Hobbiss et al, 2021).
Continuing with our professional development so we focus on improving our practice will prevent us from developing and automating bad habits, and instead promote effective teaching.

The focus (eg. setting routine homework) should have benefits for student learning and needs to be evidence-informed. It really is not a good time (probably ever) if the focus is on extensive written marking or on using a mandated powerpoint format in all subjects.

Talk to staff, really listen to any concerns and take appropriate suggestions on board. The people implementing something new will know better than someone with less teaching time if it can actually be done well.

Teaching is tough job at the best of times, teaching during a pandemic is incredibly stressful and is testing a lot of us. Despite that, there are some things we need to continue doing so we are effective at teaching and have a positive impact on our students’ learning. I would argue that it is, in fact, more important now than ever to improve our practice.
